description: We are students at Özdemir Bayraktar Aviation and Space Technologies school at Türkiye. We come together to attend Lunar Landing Site Navigator Challange. Our project is called Star Lit Path Guide System. It calculates the most suitable areas using the algorythm we made. We visualize the data we take and turn them into easy-to-read maps for easier use. Some of our skills involve Coding, Ai engineering and design.
summary: In missions that intend to land at the Moon's South Pole, determining proper landing areas and dates, and evaluating access to sunlight and solar energy, communication possibilities, and surface conditions are indispensable. Evaluating these factors jointly is essential. Changes in these factors complicate planning. Our project, Star Lit Path Guide System (SLPGS), is an interactive landing site decision-support system based on NASA datasets and astronomical calculations. The system analyses the topographic features of the Moon's South Pole, long-term sunlight availability, and permanently shadowed regions to evaluate candidate landing areas. It evaluates 10 candidate landing sites, each divided into 1,600 grid cells, resulting in a total of 16,000 grid cells. By analysing hourly conditions within a user-defined date range, it determines the most suitable site, landing time, and location. Our system shows analysis results to users via interactive maps, comparisons between candidate areas, and detailed grid visualisations. Users can examine how areas are evaluated according to different criteria and view all analysis results. Thanks to these features, complex scientific information becomes more understandable and accessible to users.
details:
SLPGS (Star Lit Path Guide System)

1. What Is SLPGS?

Project name: Star Lit Path Guide System (SLPGS)

Subtitle: Lunar South Pole Landing Site Decision Support System

SLPGS is a web-based scientific decision-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Its primary purpose is to identify favorable lunar south pole landing sites, landing dates, landing hours, and specific locations within candidate regions.

The system combines:

  • NASA lunar topography datasets.
  • Long-term solar illumination data.
  • Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) data.
  • Calculated solar and Earth geometry.
  • Multi-criteria decision analysis.
  • Interactive maps and scientific visualizations.

Our main research question:

"How can we identify suitable lunar south pole landing locations and times by considering solar energy availability, Earth communication visibility, and surface conditions together?"

SLPGS does not guarantee a safe spacecraft landing. It provides preliminary scientific evaluation and comparative decision support.

2. The Problem We Are Solving

The Moon's south pole is an important region for future lunar exploration, but landing-site selection is challenging.

Solar energy availability

Near the lunar poles, the Sun often remains close to the horizon. Solar visibility therefore changes significantly with location and time.

A landing site that performs well during one period may perform poorly during another.

Earth communication

The Earth can appear close to the lunar horizon. Its geometric visibility changes over time, affecting the potential for direct communication.

Challenging terrain

Crater rims, slopes, elevations, and rugged terrain complicate the identification of favorable landing areas.

Permanently Shadowed Regions

Some regions near the lunar poles receive extremely little or no direct sunlight. These are called Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).

They are scientifically important but introduce additional considerations for landing-site analysis.

Time-dependent conditions

The same location can have significantly different solar and Earth visibility conditions at different hours.

Our approach: Evaluate both location and time through a unified scientific scoring system.

3. Project Scope

SLPGS currently analyzes 10 candidate landing sites near the lunar south pole.

The sites are:

  1. Shackleton Rim
  2. Connecting Ridge
  3. de Gerlache Rim 1
  4. de Gerlache Rim 2
  5. Malapert Mountain
  6. Haworth Rim
  7. Nobile Rim 1
  8. Nobile Rim 2
  9. Amundsen Rim
  10. Leibnitz Beta Plateau

For each site:

  • Analysis area: 4 × 4 km
  • Grid resolution: 100 × 100 m
  • Grid dimensions: 40 × 40
  • Total cells per site: 1,600

Across the entire system:

  • 10 landing sites
  • 16,000 grid cells
  • 160 km² of total analysis area
  • Hourly analysis throughout 2027
  • 8,760 hourly samples for a full-year window

The system does not search the entire lunar surface. It compares predefined analysis regions within these 10 candidate sites.

4. NASA Data Sources

SLPGS uses actual NASA datasets, not artificially generated terrain measurements.

NASA LRO / LOLA Topography

Instrument: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA)

Spacecraft: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)

Dataset: High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites

NASA PGDA Product 78

https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/78

The system uses approximately 5 m/pixel elevation and slope products.

These datasets support:

  • Surface slope evaluation.
  • Terrain ruggedness analysis.
  • Topographic characterization.
  • NASA LOLA shaded-relief visualizations.

The 5 m elevation model contains processed/interpolated data; it does not mean every pixel represents an independent laser observation.

Lunar Polar Illumination

NASA PGDA Product 69

https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/69

Relevant dataset:

AVGVISIB_75S_120M_201608.TIF

Native resolution: approximately 120 m/pixel.

This raster represents long-term average solar visibility and contributes to estimating the illumination potential of each grid cell.

It does not directly measure actual sunlight at a specific hour in 2027.

Permanently Shadowed Regions

Dataset:

LPSR_75S_120M_201608.TIF

Native resolution: approximately 120 m/pixel.

The system uses this data to identify PSR locations and calculate proximity to designated PSR regions.

PSR proximity is not direct evidence that accessible water ice exists at a particular location.

Solar and Earth Geometry

SLPGS calculates hourly Sun and Earth positions through mathematical methods based on Jean Meeus's Astronomical Algorithms.

These are backend computations, not hourly Sun/Earth images downloaded from NASA.

The calculations include:

  • Geometric solar elevation.
  • Geometric Earth elevation.
  • Visibility above the geometric horizon.
  • Consecutive visible-hour periods.

Scientific limitation: The calculations do not model local terrain blocking the horizon.

5. How SLPGS Works

The platform uses a two-level analysis architecture.

Step 1 — Data Preparation

NASA raster datasets are processed into grid-level terrain and environmental characteristics.

Static features are cached so that the application does not need to process all the original GeoTIFF files for every request.

Step 2 — Hourly Astronomical Calculations

The backend calculates solar and Earth geometry for the selected 2027 date range.

Step 3 — Grid-Level Analysis

Each of the 16,000 grid cells is evaluated using 10 weighted scientific criteria.

Step 4 — Suitability Filtering

The system applies data-validity, physical and operational suitability requirements.

Step 5 — Site-Level Analysis

Each landing site receives a score derived from the performance and distribution of its grid cells.

Step 6 — Landing Recommendation

The system evaluates candidate site–hour combinations and identifies the highest-ranked combination that contains at least one suitable grid cell.

It then identifies the best suitable grid within the selected site.

If no qualifying solution exists, the system explicitly returns No Feasible Landing Solution.

Step 7 — Interactive Visualization

Users can inspect the selected site, compare alternatives, study individual grid cells, and explore different hours.

Suggested visual flow:

NASA Data → Grid Processing → Sun/Earth Geometry → Grid Scoring → Site Scoring → Landing Recommendation

6. Grid-Level Scoring Algorithm

Every grid cell is evaluated using 10 weighted criteria.

Scoring Criteria and Weights

  1. Continuous Sun Visibility — 20%
  2. Earth Visibility Ratio — 15%
  3. Earth Elevation at Landing — 10%
  4. Long-Term Illumination — 10%
  5. Sun Visibility Ratio — 10%
  6. Continuous Earth Visibility — 10%
  7. Surface Slope — 10%
  8. Sun Elevation at Landing — 5%
  9. Terrain Ruggedness Index — 5%
  10. PSR Distance — 5%

These criteria are normalized to a 0–100 scale and combined into a weighted grid score.

Thematic priorities:

  • Solar-related criteria: 45%
  • Earth communication-related criteria: 35%
  • Terrain-related criteria: 15%
  • PSR proximity: 5%

Solar and Earth geometry together represent 80% of the grid score, reflecting our project's focus on energy availability and direct Earth visibility.

These weights are project design decisions, not official NASA engineering standards.

Suitability Requirements

A cell is classified as suitable only if it satisfies the model's requirements.

Main conditions include:

  • Slope ≤ 10°.
  • Cell center is outside PSR.
  • Grid score ≥ 68/100.
  • Sun is above the geometric horizon at the selected landing hour.
  • Earth is above the geometric horizon at the selected landing hour.
  • Required data are valid.

The system distinguishes between:

  • Suitable.
  • Feasible but not suitable.
  • Physically infeasible.
  • Invalid / missing data.

Important: These are SLPGS model classifications and do not certify real-world landing safety.

7. Site-Level Scoring

SLPGS does not select a landing region solely because it contains one high-scoring cell.

Each site is evaluated through four components.

Site Criteria and Weights

  1. Mean Grid Score — 40%
  2. Suitable Grid Ratio — 25%
  3. Largest Connected Suitable Area — 20%
  4. Grid Score Consistency — 15%

Mean Grid Score: Represents the average performance of valid cells.

Suitable Grid Ratio: Represents the proportion of cells satisfying the suitability requirements.

Largest Connected Suitable Area: Measures the largest connected group of suitable cells using four-neighbor adjacency. The area component reaches its maximum score at 1 km².

Grid Score Consistency: Uses the variation of grid scores to evaluate how uniform the site's conditions are.

The final site score combines all four components.

This approach evaluates the overall quality and spatial distribution of favorable cells instead of relying on a single exceptional location.

8. Main Website Features

The SLPGS website contains the following features.

Mission Control

Users select an analysis date range, run scientific calculations, and receive a recommended landing location and time.

Lunar South Pole Map

An interactive lunar south pole map displays the 10 candidate regions.

The overview uses real NASA LOLA topographic relief and a lunar south-polar stereographic projection.

Users can select sites and navigate to detailed grid analysis.

Site Comparison

The system supports two comparison approaches:

Same Hour for All Sites: All candidate regions are evaluated at the same inspection hour.

Each Site's Own Best Hour: Each site is compared at its own optimal hour within the selected analysis window.

These are different comparisons and must not be confused.

Interactive Grid Heatmap

Each landing site contains an interactive 40 × 40 grid map.

The user can inspect 12 data layers, including total score, suitability, Sun/Earth visibility, slope, terrain ruggedness, and PSR distance.

The heatmap can display actual NASA LOLA shaded relief beneath the grid.

Grid Scientific Details

Selecting an individual cell reveals:

  • Grid ID and coordinates.
  • Total grid score.
  • Raw scientific values.
  • 10 criterion scores.
  • Criterion weights and contributions.
  • Suitability classification.
  • Reasons for exclusion.
  • Landing-hour geometric conditions.
  • Geometric visibility durations following landing, where available.

Time Explorer

An interactive time-series visualization allows users to inspect how a site's performance changes.

Displayed metrics include:

  • Site score.
  • Best grid score.
  • Suitable grid count.
  • Mean grid score.
  • Suitable grid ratio.
  • Connected-area score.
  • Consistency score.

Users can choose different dates and hours. The grid, site comparison, and scientific details update according to the selected inspection time.

Science & Transparency

The Science & Transparency section explains the project's methodology, scoring system, data sources, assumptions, and scientific limitations.

9. Software Architecture

The SLPGS application consists of two major components.

Backend

Technology: Python + FastAPI.

Algorithm version: 2.1.0.

Responsible for:

  • NASA raster preprocessing.
  • Terrain feature extraction.
  • Hourly Sun/Earth calculations.
  • Scientific scoring.
  • Suitability filtering.
  • Site ranking.
  • Recommendation selection.
  • REST API responses.

Frontend

Technology: React + TypeScript + Vite.

Responsible for:

  • Interactive interface.
  • Date selection.
  • Site and grid maps.
  • Time-series charts.
  • Result visualization.
  • User navigation.
  • Scientific explanations.

Crucial architecture rule: The frontend does not independently calculate landing rankings or scientific scores. It visualizes results generated by the Python backend.

10. Real Analysis Examples

The platform has been tested with real NASA-derived data and a functioning backend.

Example A — April 2027

Analysis window: March 26 – April 26, 2027.

Recommended site: Nobile Rim 2

Recommended landing hour: April 13, 2027 — 03:00 UTC

Site score: 49.0 / 100

Best grid: r005c017

Best grid score: 71.8 / 100

Example B — July 2027

Analysis window: July 1–31, 2027.

Recommended site: Haworth Rim

Recommended landing hour: July 24, 2027 — 22:00 UTC

Site score: 51.3 / 100

Best grid: r032c038

Best grid score: 73.4 / 100

Example C — Full Year 2027

Recommended site: Nobile Rim 2

Recommended landing hour: February 14, 2027 — 03:00 UTC

Site score: 64.8 / 100

Best grid: r005c017

Best grid score: 77.6 / 100

These examples demonstrate that optimal recommendations depend on the selected time window.

Use them only as documented results from our tested SLPGS version, not as NASA-certified landing recommendations.

11. Scientific Validation

Scientific validation is a major part of our project.

Our independent validation work included:

  • Comparison of 42 Sun/Earth angle pairs against JPL Horizons for selected site-time combinations.
  • Agreement in all 42 geometric above/below-horizon classifications.
  • Maximum reported elevation discrepancy of approximately 0.027°.
  • Maximum reported azimuth discrepancy of approximately 0.010°.
  • Inspection of NASA raster metadata.
  • Structural checks of the prepared datasets.
  • Sensitivity analysis of scoring behavior and ranking stability.

Overall scientific assessment: Partially Verified.

This is important: geometric agreement with JPL Horizons does not establish that local terrain obstruction, landing safety, solar panel power output, or radio-link quality have been validated.

Do not present validation as NASA endorsement.

The scientific validation report and supporting results will be included in the GitHub repository.

12. Scientific Limitations

The website must explicitly acknowledge the following:

Terrain occlusion: Local crater rims or mountains may obstruct the Sun or Earth even when the calculated geometric elevation is positive.

Solar power: Geometric sunlight visibility does not directly determine actual photovoltaic energy output.

Communication: Geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee a reliable radio link.

Spatial resolution: The 100 m analysis grid combines datasets with different native resolutions, including 5 m topography and 120 m illumination/PSR products.

PSR interpretation: Proximity to permanent shadow does not prove water-ice availability.

Model parameters: The scoring weights and thresholds are project-specific assumptions rather than universally accepted NASA landing standards.

Geographic coverage: The system evaluates 10 predefined 4 × 4 km regions rather than conducting an unrestricted global search.

Temporal resolution: Calculations use one-hour samples.

Time-window limits: Visibility durations may be truncated by the chosen analysis interval.

Landing safety: SLPGS is a preliminary decision-support and scientific visualization tool, not an operational spacecraft guidance system.

13. What Makes SLPGS Distinctive?

Highlight these main contributions:

  1. Integrated spatial and temporal analysis: Site selection and landing-hour selection are addressed together.
  2. Two-level scientific assessment: 10 candidate sites and 16,000 grid cells.
  3. Energy and communication priorities: Solar and Earth-related factors receive 80% of the combined grid weights.
  4. Region-level suitability: Site ranking considers overall cell performance and the distribution of suitable areas.
  5. Explainable calculations: Users can inspect individual criterion values, weights, and scores.
  6. Interactive scientific exploration: Time Explorer, layered grid maps, site comparison, and NASA LOLA relief.
  7. Scientific transparency: Assumptions, data sources, and limitations are made visible.

We are not claiming to have invented lunar illumination modeling or independently discovered all candidate regions.

Our contribution is the integration of established scientific data and methods into an accessible, explainable, interactive landing-site decision-support platform.

Deployment Platforms Used to Publish Our Website:
